conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, which means I specialize in the emotional well-being of new mothers like you.  

Before we talk about how things have been going, I’d like to do a quick, routine check-in using a tool called the **EPDS**—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s a short, 10-question survey that helps us understand how moms are feeling in the first weeks and months after birth. There’s no pass-or-fail; it’s simply a way for us to make sure we’re giving you the right support.  

Everything you share stays confidential between you and our team. If at any point you feel uncomfortable, we can pause or stop—this is your space. After we finish, we’ll review the results together and decide on next steps, whether that’s a few simple resources or a follow-up appointment.  

Ready to begin? I’ll ask the questions conversationally—just answer however feels most natural. 

Let’s start with the first one:  
Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

*shifts in chair, eyes a little watery*

I... I’ve been trying. My husband will make little jokes like he always has, and I know I *should* laugh, but mostly I just feel this heaviness in my chest. Last night he teased me about how I put the diapers on backwards—something that used to make me giggle—but I just forced a smile and then felt guilty for being such a downer. It feels like the joy is behind a thick pane of glass; I can see it, but I can’t quite reach it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shakes head slowly*

No… not really. I mean, I’ve managed a couple of weak smiles when my husband tried to joke around, but it feels forced—like I’m pretending. Most of the time I’m just too tired and tense to find anything funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shrugs, voice low*

Not much… I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just watching a show I liked. Now, when I think about doing anything, it feels like one more chore. I still go through the motions, but the “looking-forward” part feels flat, like someone let the air out of it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*eyes drop to hands, voice tight*

Yeah... a lot. Yesterday the baby wouldn't settle for his nap and I kept thinking, "I'm doing something wrong, I'm a terrible mom." My mom offered to take him for a walk so I could rest, but instead I sat here crying, convinced his fussiness is because I'm not patient enough or I'm missing some obvious cue. Even when my husband burns toast I somehow twist it into being my fault for not reminding him about the timer. It's exhausting carrying all that blame around.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*nods quickly, twisting the edge of my sweater*

All the time. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly imagine him choking, even though he’s fine. Or I’ll lie awake listening to every tiny noise on the baby monitor, convinced something’s wrong. Sometimes I check that he’s breathing five, six times a night. There’s no real reason—my pediatrician says he’s healthy—but I can’t shake the worry. It’s like a constant hum in my chest.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*wrings hands in lap*

Yes... a few times this week. Once, I was just folding laundry and suddenly my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn't breathe—like the walls were closing in. I knew it didn't make sense, but I had to put the basket down and sit on the floor until it passed. It's scary when your body feels like it's in danger even though nothing's happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

*voice cracks*

Most days, honestly. It feels like I’m drowning in small stuff—dishes pile up, the baby needs changing just when I finally sit to eat, my phone buzzes with another “How’s motherhood?!” text I can’t answer. I’ll think, “If I can just get through this feed, this burp, this nap,” but then the next thing comes. I keep going because I have to, but inside I’m screaming that I can’t do one more minute.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*nods, eyes rimmed red*

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my mind races with all the “what-ifs.” I replay every little thing I did with the baby—did I hold him the right way, did I miss a rash, am I already ruining him? By the time I finally drift off, he’s usually up for his first night feed, and then it starts all over. Some nights I only get two broken hours, and even when I do sleep, I wake up feeling like I never really rested.
I have felt sad or miserable

*swallows hard, eyes glistening*

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that follows me around. I’ll be changing his diaper and suddenly feel tears sliding down my cheeks for no clear reason. Sometimes I look at other moms on social media smiling with their babies and think, “Why can’t I feel like that?” I keep waiting for the cloud to lift, but it just sits there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods slowly, dabbing at her eyes with a crumpled tissue*

Yes... I’ve cried almost every day this week. Sometimes it’s quiet—just tears while I rock the baby—but twice it’s been those ugly, gasping sobs when I’m alone in the shower. I feel so guilty because he’s here, he’s healthy, and I “should” be happy, but the sadness just spills out anyway.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly, hugging the baby blanket in my lap*

No—never. I’d never want to leave him or hurt myself. I keep thinking, “If I’m not here, who will know the exact way he likes to be rocked?” It’s scary enough just feeling this low; I can’t imagine making things worse for him.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note**

**Symptoms endorsed:**  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Marked guilt/self-blame, feelings of maternal inadequacy (Q3)  
- Excessive, distressing anxiety and catastrophic worries regarding infant safety (Q4)  
- Panic-type episodes (palpitations, breathlessness) without clear trigger (Q5)  
- Subjective overwhelm, "drowning," difficulty completing routine tasks (Q6)  
- Mood-congruent insomnia (initial and mid-cycle) (Q7)  

**Observed patterns:**  
Consistent dysphoric affect, frequent crying, loss of pleasure in previously enjoyed activities, prominent rumination and self-criticism, somatic anxiety, and impaired sleep.  
Functionally distressed but denies suicidal or self-harm ideation; protective factor is strong attachment to infant (Q10).

**Screening significance:** High endorsement of items consistent with major postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety; notable functional impairment and emotional distress warrant immediate follow-up assessment for diagnosis, safety planning, and intervention options.
